newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. cautious about Tajikistan shooting report.
newsitem.headline: U.N. cautious about Tajikistan shooting report.

text.p: The United Nations said on Thursday it could not get independent confirmation of reports that Tajikistan rebels killed a U.N. military observer among their dozen hostages.

The Itar-Tass news agency said one of its correspondents, herself a hostage held near Obigarm in the Central Asian country, had reported by satellite phone to her Moscow office that a U.N. military observer had been shot and killed.
But U.N. spokesman Yasuhiro Ueki said that despite repeated attempts "we cannot confirm the report and are checking."

The Tajik government earlier on Thursday said it flew in 40 rebels from Afghanistan ahead of a rebel deadline for a prisoner swap, but government spokesman Zafar Saidov said their release was delayed by haggling.
Diplomatic sources, however, said they understood the exchange did not come off because the rebels had increased their demands and now wanted more than 100 people flown in.
Consequently, they viewed the reports with caution, speculating that the rebels had either killed the observer to emphasise their demands or had lied about killing him for the same reason.

The hostages include three U.N. military observers -- two Swiss and a Ukrainian -- four Russian reporters and four workers with the U.N. refugee agency. The rebels also seized Tajikistan's security minister on Saturday when he flew in to negotiate the captives' release.

In Switzerland, a defence ministry spokesman called the report that a hostage had been killed "not credible" and said the Swiss government was still seeking information from Tajikistan and from United Nations.

Another journalist hostage, from Interfax, also reported the shooting. Both reporters have sent frequent stories from captivity, but it is not clear to what extent they are reporting what their captors tell them to say.

Tajkistan, since the breakup of the Soviet Union has suffered a mosaic of clan and regional rivalries, in which tens of thousands of people were killed, 600,000 were displaced and another 300,000 fled to Afghanistan and Russia.
